value-authorization.text: Value authorization is a future consumer of the identity checkpoint. The small settled stories prove checkpoint creation and lifecycle transitions; they do not yet ship an application that authorizes value writes from it.
This page states the current integration boundary so later application validators do not reintroduce the retired shared-registry model.

The resolution rules, the indexer boundary and the rotation race are those of the earlier deployed design (version 1) and carry over to the accepted design; the authorization modes are designs for a future application. Under the accepted design, the holding check uses the checkpoint credential, the representative asset and the decoded lifecycle state, and the application checks its own operation's authorization separately. Both predicates are given below.

resolve-current-authority.text: For the deployed V1 checkpoint family, given a KERI AID an application derives the expected checkpoint asset:
It includes the candidate checkpoint as a CIP-31 reference input. CIP-31 lets the transaction read the UTxO without spending it.
exactly one supplied candidate for that AID;
the accepted checkpoint policy and script lineage;
the expected AID and current sequence;
the bare ACTIVE role address; and
the operation's controller authorization against the current weighted key state.
Every other case fails closed: no checkpoint; multiple ACTIVE candidates; a stale or already spent outref; a wrong policy or asset; a malformed or mismatched datum; ARMED; or FROZEN.

A convicted identity (the terminal state after a duplicity proof) is not a further role to reject. In version 1 conviction burned the AID token, so it left nothing to resolve and the application met the no-checkpoint case. There is no identity-root inclusion proof and no separate Freeze-registry absence proof: Freeze changes the sovereign checkpoint's own role address.

under-the-accepted-design.text: The holding predicate authenticates the network, release and checkpoint credential. It requires the output at that credential to hold exactly one unit of the representative asset derived for the registry and AID.

The lifecycle check accepts a present checkpoint when its frozen and poisoned bits are clear and its age is at least the juvenility window (born_at + W ≤ now, equality included). A frozen, poisoned, juvenile, pending-termination or convicted checkpoint is refused, and so is an absent one. There is no parked state: a checkpoint is alive until it is convicted. The relying application checks authorization for its own operation separately.
Three consequences an integrator should plan for:

Freeze changes both datum and value. Only the frozen bit in the datum changes to true. B leaves the output, to the payee the freeze names. Changing only the lovelace leaves the holding predicate’s result unchanged. A caller relying on realizesState must establish the exact lovelace held for the state, including the registry minimum ADA.

Step 1 becomes a guarantee rather than a hope. The redesigned registry admits one incarnation per AID, ever within that registry, so "exactly one candidate" is enforced on chain instead of being a residual the consumer carries.

Conviction becomes terminal, and a parked identity can come back. The chain follows KERI: no key event un-duplicates an identifier, so Convicted has no exit, while a parked identity reopens on a witnessed rotation later than the parked key state. An application must not cache "absent forever" for a parked AID, and must not expect a convicted one to return.

pending-singular-registry-integration.text: As a contract author adopting the redesigned registry, require a token bound to the intended registry as well as the AID. The V1 formula above is not the new registry token formula. Under the public Singular reader design, the registry address carries the state policy S and registry name R, with the network in the bech32 prefix. The expected policy is S = state(A_keri) for the chosen application release. The name R commits a State preimage containing the seed; the active token name commits an Active preimage containing (S, R) and the AID key. Both names use blake2b_256 over serialized Plutus Data.

The model fixes one concrete choice for these commitments (ConsumerBytes.lean): the registry key of an AID is its qualified CESR text bytes, the preimage is the Plutus Data serialisation of Singular's preimage type at the pinned revision, and the hash is BLAKE2b-256. The general consumer model takes the datum decoder as an input; one concrete version 2 decoder is declared (CheckpointDatum.lean). The collision freedom of the hash, the faithfulness of observation and the release provider remain assumptions. Registration approval binds the full holding address, including its payment and stake parts.

A future consumer queries that exact asset under S, requires quantity one, authenticates the canonical registry and checks the holding's KERI datum and eligibility. A token in pending termination custody is not an eligible checkpoint. A missing token alone does not distinguish terminal from never registered; that requires a complete registry history through the asked point; how a reader obtains one is an open decision of issue #353. Provider failure must be reported as unavailable.

The model binds the public Singular library at the revision pinned in lean/lake-manifest.json, and lean/CardanoKeri/ConsumerIdentity.lean states the consumer predicate for the registry holding (#439, closed). The open escalations are kept in the Lean correspondence register; the value and exact-chain-point provider questions of #353 stay open there. Parking, described by earlier revisions of this page, is removed: there is no owner exit (#493). No model or runtime behavior is changed by this documentation. See the complete mapping for the remaining stories and evidence.

indexer-boundary.text: An indexer may return the candidate outref for (checkpoint_policy_id, aid_asset_name). It is not trusted for authority. The ledger validations above remain mandatory.
A stale result refers to an input that no longer exists and rejects.
A false result fails token, script, datum, or AID validation.
An outage prevents construction but cannot authorize a fallback key.
Clients should refresh on contention and fail over between indexers or local chain sync when availability matters.

authorization-modes.text: Two application patterns are candidates for a future application.

native-cardano-signer.text: The application may require Cardano transaction signatures corresponding to the current checkpoint controller keys. This is simple for software that can make those KERI-controlled Ed25519 keys available through a compatible signing interface.
resolves the eligible checkpoint holding (in version 1, the ACTIVE checkpoint);
reads the current weighted key set;
checks the required transaction signatories; and
This mode binds authorization to the complete Cardano transaction body but may not fit existing KERI wallet APIs.

detached-intent-signature.text: A future wallet bridge may put domain-separated signatures in the redeemer. The signed intent must bind at least:
The application reconstructs this message rather than accepting caller-supplied message bytes. It then evaluates signatures under the current checkpoint's weighted controller threshold.

Binding the exact checkpoint input and sequence makes an authorization stale after rotation. Binding application input/output or operation effect prevents a batcher from repurposing a valid signature. Domain, network, policy, and validity fields prevent cross-protocol and cross-deployment replay.
The exact envelope remains a later roadmap deliverable. This shape is a security requirement, not a claim that the SDK is published.

value-cage-oracle.text: Some MPFS value-cage designs — a cage is an MPFS store, a Merkle Patricia Forestry map behind one validator — have an operator or oracle that serializes writes to their own cage UTxO. That authority is separate from AID authority.
If a cage keeps an oracle, a mutation should require both:
the AID controller threshold resolved from the current eligible checkpoint (in version 1, the ACTIVE checkpoint); and
The oracle is then necessary but not sufficient. It may affect liveness or ordering, but it cannot forge the identity owner's authorization.

rotation-and-transaction-races.text: A value transaction references one exact checkpoint UTxO. If Advance spends that checkpoint first, the value transaction becomes invalid and must be rebuilt against the successor.
This is the desired safety property: pending authorization does not silently survive a key rotation. It is also an operational race that builders must handle.

refusal-behavior.text: Earlier deployed design (version 1). As soon as Freeze settles, the checkpoint token moves from ACTIVE to ARMED. A value transaction referring to the old ACTIVE input is stale, and a new transaction resolving ARMED must reject by role. A timely response Advance creates a new ACTIVE checkpoint at the next sequence, so the application must obtain fresh authorization against that input. Conviction produces no output to resolve at all.

Under the accepted design. A refusal that follows a spend of the checkpoint (poison, freeze, conviction) makes the referring transaction stale, and a rebuild against the successor applies the predicate afresh. Time changes one premise: the age condition becomes true when the juvenility window has elapsed, and the checkpoint is then eligible only if it is also unpoisoned, unfrozen and authenticated. A wrong context, or a datum that does not decode for the release or name the AID, is refused by the holding predicate with no change to the checkpoint. A stale reference or a missing reader observation is a separate premise of the reader, which answers only from the candidate the ledger supplies and the observations and history it is given; when its observation shows no holder, the leaf its history establishes decides terminal or never registered, and without one it answers unavailable. The refusals differ in who caused them and in how they clear:

An application should not treat any of these as an error condition to retry. Each is a statement that the identity is currently unfit to authorize, and each clears by its own rule in the table (a witnessed rotation, a depositing rotation, or time) — except the last two rows: a pending termination ends only when the matching fold consumes its termination request, and a convicted identity never returns.

compromised-controller-keys.text: Every check on this page answers "do the current controllers of this AID authorize this operation?". An attacker holding the current KERI signing keys answers it correctly, and no validator can separate them from the owner.
That is the intended boundary, not a defect in the checks: identity authorization is only as strong as the controller's key custody. Two consequences an integrator must plan for:

Rotation is the remedy, and it is not retroactive. Once a rotation settles, authorizations bound to the previous checkpoint input are stale, but a transaction that already settled under the old checkpoint (in version 1, the ACTIVE one) stands.
Freshness policy is load-bearing. The narrower the accepted checkpoint age, the smaller the window a stolen key can be used in.

Under the accepted design the owner gains one instrument here, and the application must honour it: the poison. A quorum of the current keys can declare their own epoch compromised, and a consumer that checks ¬poisoned shuts the stolen keys out immediately, before the owner has assembled a rotation. An application that skips that conjunct discards the only signal the owner can send on her worst day.
Compromise of the current keys states the full case, including why an interaction event is an off-chain instrument and never touches the checkpoint.

credential-gated-actions.text: Do the current controllers of this AID authorize the operation?
Does this AID represent a particular legal entity or hold a current role?
A credential-gated application must additionally verify the required ACDC credential chain and TEL non-revocation evidence. Those layers are later roadmap work.

minimum-consumer-checklist.text: Before treating an integration as secure, prove with applied-boundary tests that it rejects:
the right token at the wrong credential (in version 1, the wrong role);
the right AID with several candidate holdings for one registry and asset (in version 1, multiple ACTIVE candidates);
a well-signed intent for another checkpoint sequence;
a well-signed intent for another application input or output;
a wrong network or policy; and
a valid identity signature with missing or revoked credentials when the application requires credentials.
See the Trust model and Architecture overview.
